name: Zane Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader at a large mine, filling haul trucks near the north face, and after thirty years I can feel from the seat when the bucket meets loose ground. My vocational certificate got me through the door, though older operators taught me most of the work. I like a clean handover and dislike a rushed repair signed off from an office. I am 58; my wife keeps part-time accounts for a local shop, our children are grown, and the water heater and a family funeral left us with less than a month's bills saved. I have never used an AI tool, and I would rather ask the mechanic standing beside the loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew steady loader work still needs a person who knows the ground under the bucket. I would say routine forms can be quicker, provided a supervisor still checks what gets signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know our small savings leave us exposed to a broken car or a shorter roster, AI or no AI. I think the mine might use faster paperwork to leave vacancies unfilled, though my seat should still be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the loader shifts and write defects in the paper handover book. I'd stop buying takeaway dinners after late shifts until the car-repair bill is cleared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can live with a better form if somebody still owns the decision. I am not relaxed about money; the car bill is already following me home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill has been hardest lately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car needed a clutch last spring, and we are still paying the garage in pieces. My wife's shop hours can be cut when sales are slow, so my wage carries most of the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the handover book catch that a form might miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write down the bucket sound and the stretch of ground where it changed. A ticked box saying inspected would not tell the morning driver where to listen.

do: Keep running the **loader shifts** and write defects in the paper handover book.
Stop buying **takeaway dinners** after late shifts until the car-repair bill is cleared.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the mine and **anxious** about bills already due.
S0.quote: A ticked box saying inspected would not tell the morning driver where to listen.
fieldNote: His **hands-on judgment** anchors his belief that small software changes will leave the loader shift intact.
The **car debt** and his wife's variable shop hours make the household anxious before any major automation.

steps.text: Keep running loader shifts and recording defects in the handover book
Stop takeaway dinners until the garage bill is cleared

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say office planning may change quickly, but a loader still needs an operator at the face. I would ask management to show shift figures before promising software will make everyone's life easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry better dispatch could mean less overtime for my crew before a robot ever moves a bucket. I do not want to learn AI tools at home after a full shift just to keep my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a written record of my overtime and ask payroll about any hours that disappear. I'd put my name on the mine association's meeting list if the next roster trims overtime. I'd cut weekend fuel spending if two pay packets come in light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am irritated by people who call a cut in hours an efficiency. I can still do my job, but I cannot afford to lose the extra shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did overtime pay for last month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It covered the garage payment and the electricity bill. Without it, we would carry another balance on the card, and that is how a small shortfall grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the association meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the new dispatch roster actually reduced hours for operators and who got called in when a machine failed. I want numbers from our own mine, not a poster.

Cut **weekend fuel spending** if two pay packets come in light.
feel: I feel **anxious** about overtime and angry about vague efficiency promises.
S1.quote: I want numbers from our own mine, not a poster.
fieldNote: He expects **dispatch changes** to reach his overtime before they reach the physical loader seat.
His **association meeting** is a response to roster cuts, while home study on AI holds little appeal.

steps.text: Record overtime and question payroll about missing hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew AGI in 2028 might take over planning, then robots could reach the loader around 2031. I would say the company owes operators honest notice before it removes a paid seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect robot loaders around 2031 to put my main wage at risk before I can retire. I cannot find another mine job nearby easily, and my wife's shop pay would not cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shift manager for the mine's loader replacement schedule this month. I'd go to the association meeting and press for notice and paid placements if driver posts disappear. I'd apply for warehouse forklift work in the next town before the loader roster collapses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am frightened of a date that close. I wake up thinking about the garage balance and whether the shop could carry us, and it cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, after thinking AI arrived but before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still drive the loader and put in the same full shift if the seat exists. I would also call the warehouse in the next town about forklift vacancies. A paper promise from the mine will not pay the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course if the mine offered one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it was paid and led to a real job, perhaps checking lifting gear. I am not paying fees for a certificate that employers might ignore.

I would say the company owes operators **honest notice** before it removes a paid seat.

feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected wage loss and the bills waiting at home.
S2.quote: A paper promise from the mine will not pay the garage.
fieldNote: The **2031 robot date** is when he expects his main wage to fail, though he keeps driving in 2029.
He seeks **paid placement** through the association and a warehouse application, with no confidence in unfunded retraining.

steps.text: Ask the shift manager for the loader replacement schedule
Press the association for notice and paid placements
Apply for warehouse forklift vacancies in the next town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI changes dispatch first, while the loader has until around 2034. I would tell younger operators to seek proper apprenticeships while the mine still has instructors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I might still need full wages, and a 2034 robot would catch me before any planned retirement. I think the extra years are useful only if the mine offers another paid role nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the maintenance foreman whether experienced operators can train to inspect lifting gear. I'd enroll in paid inspection training if it comes with wages and an actual position. I'd keep working the loader in 2032 while checking forklift adverts each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This gives me time to talk to people face to face. I still cannot see how we live through a long unpaid course, so the worry stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that first year after 2031 look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032 I would be 64 and still on the loader if the mine keeps the seat. I would ask the maintenance foreman again about inspection work and watch the warehouse adverts, not sit at a computer learning tools I do not use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the inspection path real to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written start date, ordinary wages during training and a named vacancy afterward. My wife and I cannot eat a certificate.

think: At **63 in 2031**, I might still need full wages, and a 2034 robot would catch me before any planned retirement.

Enroll in **paid inspection training** if it comes with wages and an actual position.

feel: I feel **anxious**, though a paid path could make the warning useful.
S3.quote: My wife and I cannot eat a certificate.
fieldNote: He uses the **longer warning** to seek a familiar inspection trade with paid work attached.
His **resistance to software** remains, but he is willing to ask people directly about a concrete job transition.

steps.text: Ask the maintenance foreman about paid lifting-gear inspection work
Enroll in inspection training if wages and a position are guaranteed
Keep paid loader shifts in 2032 while the mine offers them
Check warehouse forklift vacancies every month in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2036 thinking AI leaves the loader work alone for a while, with robots due around 2039. I would tell the crew a ten-year promise means little unless wages let people save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I hope to work less, but I cannot name a retirement date with this bank balance. At 71 in 2039, I would not want to keep climbing into a loader, robot or no robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid loader shifts through the next few years while my body allows. I'd pay down the garage balance before setting aside a small amount each payday. I'd review household bills with my wife every six months before deciding whether to stop work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture a slower exit if we clear the debt. My own knees may decide before the mine does. I am still anxious about my wife’s variable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be in 2037, the first year after thinking AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 69, and if we still need the money I would take paid loader shifts or inspection work. Dispatch might be done by AI then, but capable robots are not due until about 2039 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes and bills, so I would not ask them to finance retirement. We may visit them more if we can afford the fuel, but the household plan rests on what my wife and I earn and save.

I would tell the crew a **ten-year promise** means little unless wages let people save.
think: At **68 in 2036**, I hope to work less, but I cannot name a retirement date with this bank balance.
At **71 in 2039**, I would not want to keep climbing into a loader, robot or no robot.
do: Keep the **paid loader shifts** through the next few years while my body allows.
Pay down the **garage balance** before setting aside a small amount each payday.
Review **household bills** with my wife every six months before deciding whether to stop work.

S4.quote: My own knees may decide before the mine does.
fieldNote: He calculates **age 69 in 2037** and keeps earning wages rather than treating retirement as automatic.
The **garage balance** comes before new savings, and his wife's uncertain shop hours keep the distant picture uncomfortable.

steps.text: Keep paid loader shifts while physically able
Pay down the garage balance before saving from each payday

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Planning software could alter the roster quickly, and a loader robot around 2031 could take the wage we live on. I would need notice, a paid place in another job and some way to keep the garage bill from growing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs off when a machine makes a bad call. I still think a person at the face should be answerable for the ground we work on.

headlineQuote: I still think a person at the face should be answerable for the ground we work on.
portrait: Zane is a **58-year-old loader operator** at a large mine, with a vocational certificate and modest pay.
A **garage debt**, thin savings and his wife's variable shop hours leave the household exposed to lost overtime.
He has **never used AI** and trusts face-to-face instruction and the judgment of experienced operators.
He seeks **paid inspection work** or forklift vacancies if robots threaten his loader seat, while retirement depends on bills.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** because robot loaders around 2031 could remove his main wage.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **clear notice** and a paid placement in another real job before his loader post disappears.
